activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Asher skipped to the sink at summer camp. His team was about to eat watermelon. The teacher, Mia, said, "Wash your hands first, Asher."

Asher turned on the water. He rubbed his hands fast. Then he looked. There were no bubbles. He looked again. No bubbles at all.

"Where are my bubbles?" he asked.

Mia smiled. "Try the soap, little one."

Asher picked up the soap. He rubbed it on his hands. He rubbed and rubbed. Bubbles popped up, small and white. More bubbles. More and more.

"Bubbles!" said Asher. "Look, look!"

He counted with Mia. One, two, three. They counted all the way to twenty. The bubbles sat on his hands like a cozy little cloud.

Then Mia helped him rinse. The bubbles went down, down, down. His hands were clean and shiny.

At the table, Asher ate his watermelon. It was sweet. After eating, he ran back to the sink.

"My turn for bubbles!" he said. And he rubbed the soap and water, and the bubbles came again.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Mya went to the storytime room. It was her first day to get a library card. She wanted a book about trucks. She looked on the low shelf. One book, two books, three books. No trucks. She looked on the round table. No trucks there either.

A man in a striped shirt waved at her. "I am the librarian," he said. "I work here. I help people find books." Mya said, "I want trucks." The librarian walked with her to a big shelf. He pulled out a red book. Trucks! Then he pulled out a blue one. More trucks!

"Now let's make your card," he said. Mya stood very still. He typed her name. The card came out of the machine. It had a little paint spot on it, orange and shiny. Mya clapped her hands.

The librarian stamped her book. "Bring it back soon," he said. Mya hugged the book to her chest. On the way out, she saw a small striped cat sitting by the door. The cat blinked at her book. Mya whispered, "One truck book, one library card, one cat. Best day."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Luka sat in the small room at the doctor's office. He wanted to show the doctor he was a big boy. So he counted what his body could do.

"My eyes see the chart. My ears hear the beep. My nose smells the soap." The doctor smiled. Then she held up a lemon slice. "Taste this," she said.

Luka thought of orange juice. Orange juice was sweet. So the lemon would be sweet too! He put it on his tongue. His whole face scrunched up. Sour! He drank some water fast.

"Was it sweet?" asked the doctor.

"No! It was sour!" said Luka.

"Then what did your tongue do?" she asked.

"My tongue tasted the sour lemon!" He touched the lemon too. It felt bumpy and cold.

The doctor gave him a sticker. It showed a fish. "That fish can swim," said Luka. He pressed the sticker on his hand. His fingers felt it stick. At home, he would tell Mama all about his day. First eyes, then ears, then nose, then tongue. "And my hand too!" said Luka.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Jordan put on his red boot, then his other boot. "Hurry!" said Dad. "The big game is on!"

At the restaurant, a giant screen glowed. Everyone sat at one long table. The screen showed men running with a ball. Jordan looked around. The fans in blue stood up. They clapped and cheered loud.

The blue team scored. Jordan jumped up too. He clapped and yelled, "Yay, blue!"

The whole table went quiet. Then Grandpa laughed. "We like the red team, buddy!"

Jordan giggled. He had clapped for the wrong team!

The red team got the ball. They ran fast. They scored! Jordan clapped hard. Everyone at the table clapped too. The waiter brought a frozen ice pop for Jordan. It was red all the way through. Jordan held it up. "This one is mine!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Iris wanted to go to the park. It was right across the road. She could see the swings from the window.

First she had to take a bath. Dad ran the water. He put his hand under the tap. "Hot," said Dad. "We wait for it to get warm." Iris touched the cold towel. It felt cool on her toes. Dad poured the water. He checked it again. Then Iris got in. The water was warm and nice.

Iris saw a shiny cup on the side of the tub. She reached for it. "Not that one," said Dad. "It has soap and sharp bits inside." Dad put it up high. Iris splashed instead.

After the bath, Iris put on her socks. Then they went out to walk to the park. The road was busy. Cars went by fast. Iris saw the swings. She wanted to run. But she stopped at the curb. She looked up at Dad. She held out her hand.

Dad smiled. He took her hand. They crossed the road together. Iris held on tight the whole way.

At the park, Iris ran to the swings. "You did it!" called Dad. He pushed her high. Iris laughed and kicked her feet.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Liam wants to draw a cat today. He walks to the tablet shelf in the computer lab. He picks up a tablet with one hand. The tablet tips and slides. It almost falls. Liam grabs it fast with his other hand. Now he holds it with two hands. It feels tight and steady in his arms. It does not slip at all.

Liam carries the tablet to the little table. He sits down slowly. He holds the tablet flat on the table. Then he presses the round button on the bottom. The screen lights up. Liam smiles. His teacher, Miss Ana, nods from her desk.

Now Liam needs the drawing app. He taps the green square. It opens. Colors fill the screen. Liam picks the purple crayon on the screen. He draws one ear. He draws the other ear. He draws whiskers, long and wiggly. The purple cat looks sleepy.

Liam draws three more cats. The room is quiet. His friend Sofia taps her screen too. Her tablet makes a soft bird song when she picks yellow.

Then the timer on the wall beeps. Time to clean up. Liam taps the big red X. The app closes. He presses the button on the bottom. The screen goes dark. He stands up and holds the tablet with two hands, one on each side. He walks slowly to the shelf.

Liam sets the tablet down soft as a kitten. He pats it once. "Night night, cat," he says.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Madison stood at the running track. She had a red beanbag and a hoop on the grass. A little pig was printed on her shirt. Her friend Theo waved from far away.

"Watch me, Theo!" said Madison. She looked at Theo and threw. The beanbag went sideways. It missed the hoop.

"Where did it go?" Theo asked.

"It went that way," said Madison. "Next time I will look at the hoop." She held the beanbag straight in her hand. She looked at the hoop. She threw. The beanbag went in.

Theo clapped. Then he tossed her the big ball. Madison used both hands. She caught it.

"Again!" she said. Theo threw it high. She caught it again.

"Now we can go swim in the pool," said Theo. They ran off together, hand in hand.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Arlo woke up and looked out the window. The backyard was white. The swing was white. The grass was white too. "Where did my yard go?" he asked. "It is under the snow," said Mom. Arlo got his boots. Mom helped him tie the laces. She made each knot tight.

"Time for school!" said Arlo. He got his backpack. Mom shook her head. "No school today," she said. "It is a snow day. A snow day means school is closed because of snow." Arlo put down his backpack. "A snow day," he said. "Can we play in it?" "Yes," said Mom.

Arlo stomped in the snow. His boots went crunch, crunch. He picked up a handful. It was cold and soft. He dropped some on the ground. It fell in a little white pile. He picked up more and dropped it again. The pile grew bigger. "Look, Mom! More snow makes a bigger pile!" Then he pushed it and patted it. It became a round ball. "Can we make it huge?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Let's roll it."

They rolled the ball across the yard. It grew and grew. The cat, their pet, watched from the fence. The snowball was as big as Arlo now. Mom found two sticks and a carrot. Arlo pushed them in. "A snowman!" he said. He patted its round tummy. The snowman smiled with his stick arms waving in the wind.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Leon went to the hair salon with his dad. It was his very first haircut. Leon sat in a big chair. The chair went up, up, up. Then Leon saw a fish tank. It had blue fish and yellow fish. Leon turned to look at the fish. Snip, snip, went the scissors. But Leon's head turned too, and the hair came out all crooked on one side.

The hairdresser said, "Oops, little fish watcher." Leon felt worried. His dad held his hand. "The fish will wait for you," Dad said. Leon counted the fish. One, two, three fish. Then he sat very still, like a statue. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft little raindrops. This time it came out neat and even all around.

The hairdresser sprayed water. It made a mist. In the mist, Leon saw a tiny rainbow. "Look, Dad, a rainbow!" he said. Dad smiled and clapped. When the haircut was done, Leon got a sticker. He walked to the fish tank. He counted again. One, two, three fish, still swimming. Leon waved goodbye. "Bye-bye, fish," he said. "Bye-bye, rainbow." Then he and Dad went home.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Owen did not want to be at the doctor. He sat on the big bed and made a grumpy face.

"Let's play a game," said Dr. Kim. "Show me your eyes." Owen blinked his eyes. He saw a red bird outside the window. "Good looking!" said Dr. Kim.

"Now your ears." Owen heard a beep from the hall. Then he heard his tummy rumble. That made him laugh.

"Smell this," said Dr. Kim. Owen sniffed with his nose. It smelled like bread. "That is my lunch," she said, and she laughed too.

She gave Owen a little cup. He stuck out his tongue. He tasted sweet juice. "Yum," said Owen.

Then Dr. Kim touched his arm with a soft brush. Owen felt it with his skin. "You are good at this game," she said.

"But I have one more," said Dr. Kim. "Take off your shoes and socks." Owen took them off. She pointed at the floor. There was a green mat with soft bumps.

Owen stepped on it with his bare toes. The mat tickled his feet. He giggled and jumped up and down. "It is like soft grass!" said Owen. "My feet can feel too!"

"That is the best answer of the day," said Dr. Kim. She gave him two stickers. Owen put one on his toes.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Anna sat at Grandma's big table. There was warm bread in a basket. Anna took a piece and put it in her mouth.

Then Anna looked up. Grandma was quiet. Papa was quiet. Aunt May was quiet. Everyone's hands were folded. Everyone was waiting. Anna's cheeks went hot. She put her bread down on her plate.

Anna pointed at the bread. "Why is everyone waiting?" she asked.

"We say thank-you first," said Grandma. "Then we eat."

Grandma held Anna's hand. Aunt May held Anna's other hand. Papa bowed his head. "Thank you for this bread," Grandma said. "Thank you for the wheat. Thank you for the sun. Thank you for the farmer and the cow who gave us milk to drink."

"A cow helped?" whispered Anna.

"A young cow," said Grandma with a smile. "She is learning too."

Then Grandma squeezed Anna's hand. "Now we eat."

Anna picked up her bread again. It was still warm. She took a big bite.

"Next time," said Anna, "can I say the thank-you?"

Grandma nodded. "Next time it is yours."

Anna looked at the bread basket. It was empty now. But then Aunt May opened the oven door with her big mitts. Out came a whole pie.

Anna clapped her hands. "Thank you, pie!" she said.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Edouard brought his book to school. He held it tight under his arm. "Can you read my book?" he asked Miss Lila. "Yes," she said. "Let us open it at the front."

Miss Lila turned page one. Then page two. Then page three. "Look," said Edouard. "A dog! Is it a pet?" "Yes," said Miss Lila. "The words say it is a pet."

Then they came to a page with only a big picture. "Read this one!" said Edouard. Miss Lila looked and looked. "I cannot read this page," she said. "There are no words on it."

Edouard leaned close. He saw the picture. He saw no little black marks. "Where are the words?" he asked. "On the next page," said Miss Lila. She turned it. There were the words. She read them all out loud. "Again!" said Edouard. He hugged his book tight.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Claire wanted to paint a dog at daycare. But the paint cups were empty. "We will fill them later," said Miss Jo. "Painting is now," said Claire. "Now we play blocks," said Miss Jo.

Claire played the block game. She stacked them tall. Then Max came over. "I went to the park tomorrow," said Max. He stopped. He thought. "No. Yesterday. I went yesterday." "Yesterday is done," said Claire. "It is behind us." She pointed at the wall. The sun picture for yesterday was cloudy and gray. Today's sun picture was up high.

"Now it is later," said Miss Jo. She set out red paint and yellow paint. Claire sat down. She painted a big dog. It had red ears. "Today I paint," said Claire. "Tomorrow I can paint a cat." She held up her paper. "Look at my dog!"

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Zoey wanted to build a toy car at daycare. She found a small box and some cardboard. She cut four square wheels all by herself. She taped them on tight.

Zoey pushed the car on the rug. It would not go. She pulled it back and pushed again. The square wheels just slid. Why would the car not roll?

Then Zoey looked across the room. Ben had a toy truck. Its wheels were round like circles. Round wheels go round and round, she thought. She looked at her square wheels. Squares had pointy corners. Would pointy corners stop the rolling?

Zoey asked her teacher for help. The teacher was brave with the big scissors and cut four round circles. Zoey taped them on. She gave the car a push. It rolled across the rug, all the way to the fish tank. The fish wiggled at the wall. Zoey laughed and chased her car. "Go, go, go!" she said.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Elizabeth loved snack time at daycare. Today Miss Ana put green peas on every tray. One, two, three trays. Four trays with peas.

Elizabeth saw Mia look at her peas. "Yuck!" Mia shouted. Miss Ana's face went sad. Mia tried again. "No, thank you," she said, quiet and small. Miss Ana smiled. She took the peas away and gave Mia a banana instead.

Elizabeth blinked. A big shout made a sad face. A small "no, thank you" made a happy face.

Then Miss Ana held out peas to Elizabeth. Elizabeth sat up straight like a butterfly sitting on a flower. "No, thank you," she said. Miss Ana smiled big. "Would you like apple slices?" "Yes, please!" said Elizabeth.

She munched her apples. One, two, three, four slices gone. "Thank you!" she said. Miss Ana laughed. "You are welcome."

At play time, Elizabeth pretended to be a butterfly. She flapped her wings over to Mia. "Would you like a pretend flower?" she asked. "No, thank you," said Mia. "Would you like a pretend apple?" Elizabeth gasped. "Yes, please!"

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Alexander stood by the bus stop with Grandma. He held his blue coat in his hands. "Can I put it on all by myself?" he asked.

"Yes, you can try," said Grandma. Alexander pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. He pulled the coat close. The zipper was tricky. He tried once. He tried twice. Then the zipper went up, up, up. "I did it!" said Alexander. He felt like he could win a big race.

Little drops of rain began to fall. Tap, tap, tap. Alexander wondered, where could his head go? Then he saw the soft part on the back of his coat. He grabbed it and pulled it up over his head. The rain tapped on top, but his hair stayed dry. "Look, Grandma! My head is hiding!" he said. A tired little turtle walked by with a boy. The turtle had a shell over its back. "The turtle has a coat too," said Alexander. The bus came, and they climbed on together.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. First, Olivier went to the airport with Mama. They stood in the arrivals area. That is where families wait for people coming off a plane.

Olivier watched the big doors. The doors opened. A man in a red hat came out. "Grandpa!" said Olivier. But it was not Grandpa. The doors opened again. A lady with a big bag came out. "Grandpa?" said Olivier. It was not Grandpa either. Then the doors opened one more time. It was Grandpa! Grandpa picked Olivier up and hugged him tight.

The next day, they went to the park. Grandpa brought bread crumbs. Olivier dropped a crumb on the ground. A little pigeon ran over and pecked it up. Olivier dropped another crumb. Another pigeon came running. "I drop it, and the pigeon eats it!" said Olivier. He dropped crumbs one by one. More and more pigeons came. Soon there were pigeons all around his feet.

Grandpa laughed and laughed. "You make the pigeons come," he said. Olivier dropped one last crumb. A little brown bird flew down too. Then Olivier took Grandpa's hand and said, "Pigeons first. Swing next!"

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Henri sat at the long table in the big hall. The table sat on a hill, and from the window Henri could see the thick green grass outside. Everyone was waiting for the potluck lunch to start.

Grandma stood next to Henri. "We hold hands now," she said. "Then we say our blessing together." Henri had a spoon in his hand. He wanted to hold Grandma's hand. But his hands were full.

Henri looked at the spoon. He looked at Grandma's open hand. He put the spoon down on the table. Now his hand was free. He reached out and took Grandma's hand. She smiled at him.

Dad held Henri's other hand. Everyone at the table held hands. They closed their eyes. They said the blessing together. Henri said the words he knew. His voice was small but clear.

Then everyone said, "Amen," and picked up their spoons. Henri picked up his spoon too. "I did it," he said. Grandma gave him a warm hug.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Sofia carried her little blue bag to the pool. The pool was right by the beach. The sand was warm. The water looked so big and shiny. "Today I will learn to swim!" said Sofia.

She ran to the pool. A boy was standing by the door. "Stop!" said the lifeguard. "Shower first!" Sofia looked at the shower. "Why do I need a shower?" she asked. "I am going to get wet anyway!" The lifeguard smiled. "Pools ask swimmers to shower first. Go on, try it."

Sofia stood under the shower. Water ran down her arms. It was warm and tickly. Then she stepped into the pool. The water felt just right. Her teacher held her hands. Sofia kicked her legs. Splash, splash, splash! "I am swimming!" she shouted. A furry dog watched from the beach. It wagged its tail.

"Did you see me?" Sofia called to her mom. "I showered, and then I swam!" Her mom clapped and waved.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Bennett stood in the pool changing room. He pulled his small blue bag. He wanted to get to the water fast. "Swim time!" he said. He started to run.

"Walk, please," said Dad. Bennett stopped. Why walk? The pool was right there! Bennett looked down. The floor was wet. It was shiny and slick.

Bennett took one big step. His foot slid a little. Whoa! The wet floor was slippery. Walking kept him steady. Step, step, step. His feet stayed right under him.

Bennett kept walking all the way to the pool. He held Dad's hand. Would the pool floor be slippery too? Bennett put one toe in the water. Then he splashed his whole foot. "The water is warm!" he said.

Dad laughed. Bennett laughed too. He would walk on wet floors. And he would swim and swim.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Anna jumped up and down. "Grandma, what will we do?"

"We will make my special bread," said Grandma. "My mama made it too."

Anna clapped her hands. "I want to help!"

Grandma put flour in a big cup. Anna poured it in the bowl. Plop! Flour dust went everywhere. "How messy!" said Anna. She laughed and laughed.

"Now we mix," said Grandma. Anna stirred the sticky dough. Round and round she went.

"Can I touch it?" asked Anna.

"Yes, squish it," said Grandma. Anna squeezed the dough. It was soft like a pillow.

Grandma put the pan in the hot oven. "You stay back here," she said. Anna watched from her stool.

The kitchen began to smell warm and sweet. Anna sniffed and sniffed. "Grandma, it smells so good!"

Ding! The bread was done. Grandma set it on the counter. Anna waited until it cooled.

Then Grandma tore a piece and handed it over. Anna took a big bite. "Mmm!" she said. "Grandma's bread!"

"Now you know my way," said Grandma. "One day you will make it too."

Anna hugged the warm loaf. "Tomorrow can we make it again?"

Grandma smiled. "Yes, my little baker."

story:

Brielle and Mama went outside to play. The wind began to blow. It blew her hair. It blew the leaves. Then it blew her hat right off her head!

"My hat!" said Brielle. The hat went fast across the grass. It rolled and tumbled. Brielle ran after it. The wind pushed it more. Brielle ran faster. At last the hat stopped by a bush. Brielle picked it up and held it tight.

Rain pitter-pattered on the glass. Brielle put her nose close to the window. A drop ran down the other side. "Hello, rain," said Brielle. She waved at the drop. It slid past her finger like it wanted to play.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:

"Why is everyone here?" Eliana asked. "Is it a party for the balloons?"

Grandma laughed softly. She took a photo from her bag. "Look at this little baby," she said.

Outside, snow began to fall past the window. Dad carried in the cake. He lit three little candles. Everyone sang.

Eliana blew them out. Then she took Grandma's hand and they slid across the smooth floor, all the way to the cake table.

"I want to see the baby photo again," she said.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Elliot wanted a tea party. He wanted a big one, with all his toys. He looked in the toy box. Out came Bear. Out came Duck. Out came Bunny too. He set them in a circle on the rug.

Then came the problem. Where was the tea? Elliot ran to the kitchen. He asked Daddy for tea. Daddy said the kettle was too hot for little hands. Elliot felt sad. A tea party needs tea. Or does it?

Elliot looked at his tea set. The little cups were empty. He picked up the teapot anyway. He tipped it over Duck's cup. He made a pouring sound. "Glug, glug, glug." Nothing came out. But Elliot said, "Tea for you, Duck!" He tipped it again over Bear's cup. "Glug, glug, glug." "Tea for you, Bear!"

Duck got her cup first. Elliot held it up to her beak. "Sip, sip," he said. Then he said, "Careful, it's pretend hot!" He blew on the empty cup. He blew on Bear's cup too.

Then Daddy brought a plate. On it was a juicy orange, all cut up. "Real snacks for the tea party," said Daddy. Elliot clapped. Bear got a pretend cake. Duck got a pretend cake. Elliot got real orange. It was the best tea party ever. "More tea, anyone?" said Elliot. "Glug, glug, glug."

story:
Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He saw a big basket full of apples. He wanted one apple very much. He reached out and grabbed at the bin. An apple rolled onto the floor.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Grayson was going on a big trip. The car was packed. Dad put in the tent. Mom put in the snacks. Grayson put in his spotted toy dog.

The car went zoom, zoom, zoom. Then it stopped. "Oh no," said Dad. "This is not our road." Mom looked worried. Grayson looked out the window. Trees. More trees. No campsite.

Dad took out a big paper map. He spread it open. Grayson peeked at it too. The map had roads. The map had places. Grayson pointed his little finger. "There is a lake," he said. Dad looked where Grayson pointed. "Yes! The lake is by the campsite!" said Dad. He found the road to the lake. The car turned. The road went the right way.

They counted as they drove. One lake. Two tents. Three happy people. "We are here!" Grayson yelled. He hugged his spotted dog. Mom set up the tent. Grayson handed her the pegs, one by one. Dad pointed at the map on his knee. "You found our way, Grayson," he said. Grayson grinned and patted the paper.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Charlotte was getting her very first haircut. She sat on a big chair at the barbershop. The chair could roll across the floor. Charlotte liked that.

Then she saw the scissors. They were shiny and sharp. "Will it hurt?" she asked.

"Let's see," said the barber. He snipped a tiny bit of hair. Snip. Charlotte waited. Then she waited some more. "I don't feel anything," she said. "Nothing at all?"

"Nothing at all," said Mommy.

Charlotte sat up tall. "Do it again," she said. Snip, snip. She did not feel a thing. The scissors cut the hair, and the hair just fell down. It landed on her cape like soft little pieces of string.

"My bike has a weak bell," said Charlotte. "It goes ding very softly. But your scissors go snip very loud!"

The barber laughed. "You are a brave one," he said. He cut and cut. Soon Charlotte had short curls all around her face.

She looked in the mirror. "New hair!" she said. She patted her curls with both hands.

"Can we come back next time?" she asked Mommy.

Mommy smiled. "Yes," she said. "We can come back."

Charlotte rolled the big chair one little roll, then hopped down.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Grandma was making mooncakes for the festival. Luke stood on his little stool. He watched her fold the dough over the sweet filling. "Can I taste one now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Grandma. "These are for tonight."

Luke saw a mooncake on the counter. It was still warm. He reached out his hand. Grandma caught him gently. "We wait," she said. "We eat them together under the moon."

Luke wanted to wait, but it was hard. He helped instead. He pressed the dough flat. He made a small nest for the filling. Grandma put the cakes in the oven. The kitchen smelled sweet.

At last it was night. The moon was big and round. The family sat outside. The plate was full of mooncakes. Luke took one big bite. It was even better because everyone was there. "More moon!" he said. Grandma laughed and gave him another piece.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Hailey was at the grocery store with Dad. It was cold outside. Very cold.

"I want to wear my coat," said Hailey. "I will do it myself."

Dad smiled. "Okay. You try."

Hailey grabbed her red coat. She pushed her arm in. Then she pushed her other arm in too. It went into the same sleeve!

"Look, Dad! I am a one-arm girl!" She laughed and wobbled around. Her coat hung funny, like a flap.

"That is a silly coat," said Dad, laughing too.

Hailey pulled her arm out. She looked at the coat. It had two sleeves. Two!

"Where does this arm go?" she asked.

"Try the other hole," said Dad.

Hailey slid one arm in one sleeve. She slid her other arm in the other sleeve. It was true! The coat felt right now.

She pulled the zipper up. Up, up, up. It clicked at the top.

"I did it!" she said.

Then Dad held up a small juice box. "A drink for the car?"

"Yes! Can I drink it in the garden at home?"

"Sure," said Dad. Hailey zipped her coat again, just to hear the little click.

He painted blue on his paper. Then he painted yellow on top. It turned green! He was so happy. But his paper got soggy and started to break. "Oh no," he said. His hand felt sticky and stuck to the page.

Miss Amy came over. "Try this tray," she said. "It is a palette. It holds your paint. You can mix colours on it first." Jayden put yellow on the palette. He put blue next to it. He stirred them with his brush. Green!

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Henri sat on the train with Mama. The train went clack, clack, clack. Henri held his cup of milk. He drank a little sip. Outside, a sheep stood in a green field. "Where are we going?" Henri asked. "To the beach," said Mama. "We will see the big water."

The train stopped. Papa carried the bag. Henri held Mama's hand. They walked on warm sand. It went squish, squish under his feet. Far away, the water moved up and down. A big wave rolled in. Then it rolled back out. Henri saw the water go in and out, in and out.

"I want to splash now," Henri said. He let go of Mama's hand. He started to run to the water. Papa caught his hand. "Wait," said Papa. "I come to the water with you." So Henri waited. He watched the waves. His legs felt weak from waiting so long. Then Papa took off his shoes. Papa held Henri's hand tight.

They walked to the water together. A wave came up to Henri's toes. It was cold and tickly. Henri laughed and jumped. Splash, splash! Mama sat on the sand and waved. Henri waved back. "I am splashing!" he called. Papa held his hand, and the water went in and out around their feet.

story:
Hudson sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to paint grass for his sheep. But he had no green paint. He looked in the cup. Red. Yellow. Blue. No green.

Hudson scratched his head. He looked at the yellow cup. He looked at the blue cup. He dipped his brush in the yellow. He painted a big yellow blob. Then he dipped his brush in the blue. He painted right on top of the yellow blob.

He waited. He watched the paint. Slow, slow, the blob turned green. Green like the grass outside. Hudson tapped his brush on the cup. "Green!" he said. He painted long green grass for his sheep.

Then he tried again. Red and yellow made a big orange blob. He tapped his foot like a little song. Blue and red made purple. Hudson painted purple grapes next to the green grass. He held up his paper. "Look at all my colours," he said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Alice sat in her car seat. Today they were going to the farm shop. The bags in the back were heavy with apples. Alice looked out of the window. A cow stood by the fence. "We came here yesterday," said Mom. Alice remembered yesterday. Yesterday she had petted a soft sheep.

"When do we see Grandma?" asked Alice. "Tomorrow," said Mom. Alice held up one hand. She counted on her fingers. "Today, tomorrow," she said. "One, two." Then she kept going. "And five more days after that." She counted and counted. Her fingers ran out at five. She still needed more days. She held up her other hand too. "Six, seven," she said.

"Seven days," said Alice. "That is a whole week." She said it again to hear the sound in her mouth. "A week has seven days." The car went bump over a little hill. Alice's fingers went up and down.

"Now we are almost at the shop," said Mom. "Later we will buy apple juice." Alice watched the gate come closer. The cow moved its tail. "Hello, cow," said Alice. "We came yesterday, and we are here today."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Everly did not want to sleep yet. "Is it tomorrow now?" she asked.

Mom shook her head. "No, it is today. Today you played in the water. Today you tasted the lemon and made a sour face."

Everly giggled. She remembered the sour lemon. "When does tomorrow come?"

"After you sleep," said Mom.

Everly frowned. "How will I know when?"

Mom pointed at the clock on the wall. "The clock shows what time it is."

Everly looked at the clock. The short hand was at eight. "Now it is eight," she said.

"Yes. Later the hand will move. Sleep comes first."

Everly got into bed. She watched the clock. The hand did not move. She closed her eyes a little. Then she peeked again.

The hand moved a tiny bit. Everly smiled.

"Mom! It moved!"

"Shh, it is sleepy time," Mom whispered.

Everly hugged her bear. The clock ticked softly. Tick, tock, tick.

"One more peek," said Everly. The hand moved again. Her eyes closed all the way.

"Goodnight, clock," she said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Ellie sat at the dinner table. The table was warm from the pot. Dad set down her plate. The peas rolled round and round.

"Can I have a cookie now?" asked Ellie. "Not now," said Dad. "The cookie is later. Now is for dinner." Ellie put her hand on the table. The plate was hot from the pot, so she pulled her hand back fast. Dad touched the plate too. "I will wait," he said. "The plate is hot now, but it cools."

Ellie ate one pea. Then she ate three more. "Yesterday I had peas too," she said. "Yes," said Dad. "Yesterday is all done. Today is now." Ellie tapped her spoon. Tap, tap, tap. "Is tomorrow now?" she asked. "No," said Dad. "Tomorrow is after you sleep."

Ellie drew a boat on her placemat with her finger. A little boat on invisible water. "The boat sails now," she said. Dad smiled. "That is a fine boat." Ellie did not want to get upset, but she wanted the cookie very much. She ate her carrots. She ate her rice, one bite at a time.

Then her plate was empty. Dad put a cookie on her plate. "Now it is cookie time," he said. Ellie held the cookie in both hands. She took a big bite. "Now the cookie is in my tummy," she said. Dad laughed and turned off the big light. "And later," he said, "we will read your boat book."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Dylan ran to the park. The sun was warm on his face. The grass smelled fresh and green. He pushed his feet through the soft sand. He felt excited.

He saw his friend Mia by the swing. Mia wanted to go high. She kicked her legs hard. Then she jumped off too fast. She tripped and fell in the sand. Mia began to cry big tears. She looked sad.

Dylan felt scared for her. But he walked over. He sat down next to her in the warm sand. "Are you okay?" he asked. Mia stopped crying. She rubbed her knee. "It hurts a little," she said. Dylan patted her back softly. Mia gave a small smile.

Then they got up together. They walked to the sandbox. It was full of smooth sand. "Let's build a big hill," said Mia. The weather was warm and the sky was blue. They dug with their hands. Mia laughed out loud. "You are my good friend," she said.

story:
Anthony went to the library with Grandma. Yesterday he got a book about trucks. Today he wanted a book about dogs. "We can find one now," said Grandma.

Anthony saw a big rug. He saw a little chair. He saw a sign with a dog on it. One dog, two dogs, three dogs on the sign.

"Storytime starts soon," said a lady with a basket of books.

"What is soon?" Anthony asked Grandma.

"Soon means we wait a little bit," said Grandma. "We can look at trucks first."

Anthony turned one page. He turned two pages. He turned three pages. Then he heard clapping. Storytime was starting now!

Anthony sat on the rug. The lady read about a hungry dog who found a cake. "Yum, yum," said the dog in the story. Anthony laughed.

After storytime, Grandma said, "Storytime again tomorrow." Anthony smiled. "Tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow too?" he asked. Grandma held his hand. "Yes. Now let's pick your dog book."

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Sofia sat in the car seat. She held her toy rabbit by one soft ear. "Rabbit has to see the dentist too," she said. Mama smiled. "First you, then rabbit watches."

"I have a loose tooth story," said Mama. "One tooth, two teeth, twenty little teeth." Sofia counted along softly. One, two, three. The car smelled like orange peels from breakfast. Outside, a big truck went by. Vroom.

At the dentist, Sofia lay back in the chair. It went up. It went down. "Open wide," said the dentist. Sofia opened her mouth. The dentist held up a tiny mirror on a handle. It was small and shiny. He put it in Sofia's mouth. He turned it this way and that way.

"Your teeth look good," he said. "The backs too?" asked Sofia. "Yes. The mirror shows me the backs of your teeth." Sofia reached out one hand. "Can I see?" The dentist put the little mirror in her palm. Sofia looked into it. She saw her own eye, big and round. She saw rabbit's fuzzy face too.

In the car, Sofia held the mirror up to rabbit's mouth. "Open wide," she said. "One tooth, two teeth, all clean." Mama buckled the seat belt and started the car.
